props.title: 47 Meters Down
props.initialSlug: Nowhere to run, nowhere to hide.

sections.content: **47 Meters Down (2017)** (2017) marks a claustrophobic evolution in shark thriller cinema, building on the legacy of **Jaws** (1975) while adding crushing depth pressure and dwindling oxygen to amp up the tension. Director Johannes Roberts crafts a deceptively simple premise - two sisters trapped in a shark cage at crushing depths - into a masterclass of aquatic horror. The film follows the underwater survival horror path blazed by **The Abyss** (1989), but strips away the sci-fi elements for raw, primal fear.

sections.content: What sets **47 Meters Down** (2017) apart is its ruthless commitment to authenticity in depicting the dangers of deep-water diving. Unlike the genetically modified monsters of Deep Blue Sea (1999) or the revenge-driven beast of **The Meg** (2018), the film's great whites behave like actual predators. The crushing pressure, nitrogen narcosis, and rapidly depleting oxygen create a triple threat that makes the sharks almost secondary antagonists to the ocean itself.

The film spawned a spiritual sequel **47 Meters Down: Uncaged** (2019), which trades the cage premise for an underwater Mayan labyrinth but maintains the series' dedication to claustrophobic tension. This evolution mirrors how **Jaws 2** (1978) attempted to expand its predecessor's scope while keeping the core shark threat intact. The subgenre continues to evolve with entries like **Great White** (2021) finding fresh angles on shark-based survival horror. SUBHEAD: Evolution of Underwater Horror

sections.content: The technical achievements of **47 Meters Down** (2017) showcase how far underwater filming has progressed since the mechanical shark troubles of **Jaws** (1975). Modern underwater thrillers like **Black Water: Abyss** (2020) and **Underwater** (2020) build on these advances, combining practical effects with CGI to create convincing aquatic threats. The film's success also sparked renewed interest in confined-space survival horror, influencing films like **The Descent** (2005) director Neil Marshall's return to claustrophobic terror.
